title: British widow faces deportation from Sweden after 22 years
description: A 78-year-old British widow has told the BBC she is struggling to eat or sleep as the Swedish government threatens to deport her over a late post-Brex
body: A 78-year-old British widow has told the BBC she is struggling to eat or sleep as the Swedish government threatens to deport her over a late post-Brexit residence application.Joyce Thomas, a retired nurse, moved to Sweden 22 years ago with her husband, who passed away from cancer three years ago.The threat of deportation came after Swedish authorities said they should have made a formal application to stay in the country after Brexit.Thomas has since had numerous applications and appeals rejected, and Tuesday marks the latest deadline for her to leave voluntarily."This is absolute hell," she said from her home in Sweden."I can't sleep, I can't eat. You get up in the morning, you don't know what's going to happen."The Swedish migration minister told the BBC that the government would "examine whether there are measures we can take to make the process easier for those affected" by some consequences of the EU-UK withdrawal agreement.When the UK left the EU on 31 January 2020, British citizens stopped being EU citizens, which meant they could no longer stay in Sweden with right of residence status.During a transitional period, British citizens could apply for residence status under the withdrawal agreement between the UK and the EU - which ended on 31 December 2021.Thomas said she and her husband were unaware that they needed to submit an application and she was only informed of the rule once she attempted to re-enter the country in 2023.After years of appeals, the Migrationsverket, the Swedish government agency responsible for migration, told her last month that her voluntary departure deadline was 8 September.Her lawyers are arguing against the deportation, but she is still waiting to hear from the government.Thomas said the possibility of having to leave her son, grandchildren, friends and husband's grave has become too much to bear."I'm tired, I really am tired and I'm not young anymore," she said."Where is the empathy? I've lived here for more than 20 years - I've got friends, I've got family."According to Eurostat data, between 2021 and 2025, 2,490 UK nationals were ordered to leave Sweden. This is almost a third of more than 7,500 UK nationals ordered to leave the 27 EU Member States over this time period.The Migrationsverket said it could not comment on Thomas's case without her consent and did not respond to a question about how many British nationals are at risk of deportation. However, it told the Guardian last week that 458 British citizens had been deported or forcibly removed since Brexit.Last month, a family told the BBC how their father, who has dementia and vascular parkinsonism and is living in full-time care in Sweden, was also threatened with removal after more than two decades in the country.Swedish Minister for Migration, Johan Forssell, told the BBC that the current framework was implemented by a previous government and that it "will therefore look closely at the situation and examine whether there are measures we can take to make the process easier for those affected".He did not address Thomas's case directly but said "the government believes the rules should be applied generously"."The UK is a very important partner for Sweden, and we want British citizens who live and work in Sweden to be able to remain here," he said."We are currently in dialogue with the relevant Swedish authorities to get a clearer picture of what measures may be possible," he added.Håkan Svenneling, Thomas's MP from the opposition Vänsterpartiet (The Left Party), has criticised the government's "inhumane migration policy". "That is why I hope that Sunday's election in Sweden will be a turning point where the opposition can form a government and change migration policy so that Joyce and other Britons with strong ties to Sweden can stay here," he told the BBC.A spokesperson from the the UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office said: "We welcome the statement from the Swedish authorities that they will look at this issue. We are ready to support them in doing so."

schema.headline: British widow faces deportation from Sweden after 22 years

title: Fourteen go on trial over deadliest Channel small boats disaster
description: Fourteen suspected people smugglers have gone on trial in Paris for their role in the worst ever small boats disaster in the English Channel.In Novemb
body: Fourteen suspected people smugglers have gone on trial in Paris for their role in the worst ever small boats disaster in the English Channel.In November 2021, at least 30 men, women and children drowned when their motorised dinghy deflated and started taking on water halfway between France and the UK.The 14 defendants – mainly Afghan nationals – are accused of manslaughter and facilitating illegal immigration as part of an organised criminal group.Most of them deny the charges. Two of the 14, who are alleged to be leaders of the operation, remain on the run and are being tried in absentia.The boat left the French coast on the evening of 23 November 2021, but ran into difficulty in the middle of the Channel. One by one the occupants entered the water to try to lessen the weight, but succumbed to the cold and drowned. Only two men survived.According to the charge sheet, the defendants helped to launch "a small boat of poor quality, unfit to navigate at sea, overloaded and equipped with inadequate life-jackets".Twenty-seven bodies were found after the boat sank, and another four were confirmed missing.Many of the people who died were Iraqi Kurds, but others came from Somalia, Ethiopia, Egypt and Afghanistan. The youngest named victim was seven years old.

schema.headline: Fourteen go on trial over deadliest Channel small boats disaster

title: Iceland summons US ambassador over Trump's stars and stripes map
description: Iceland has summoned the US ambassador after President Donald Trump posted a map on social media that appeared to show Iceland and several other count
body: Iceland has summoned the US ambassador after President Donald Trump posted a map on social media that appeared to show Iceland and several other countries covered by the American flag. Trump posted the image on Truth Social on Monday, showing the US, Canada, Greenland, Iceland, Mexico, Central America and the Caribbean covered in stars and stripes. The entire landmass was labelled "United States of America".Iceland's foreign minister said the post was "completely inappropriate".Trump's territorial ambitions have repeatedly strained relations with neighbouring countries, including his push to acquire Greenland and calls to make Canada the America's 51st state.His post of the map did not include a caption and preceded a  flurry of posts of maps renaming the US state of New Mexico as "New America". Responding to Trump's post, Iceland's Foreign Minister Þorgerður Katrín Gunnarsdóttir called in US ambassador to Iceland Billy Long, who formally took up the post last month, local media reported.When an ambassador is summoned, it typically means they are being called for a formal meeting, where the host country will express displeasure over their government's actions.The post also drew criticism from Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, who said on Monday that the position of Greenland's government and people had been made clear."The Greenlandic government and the Greenlandic people have said again and again that they do not want to be American," she told Danish news agency Ritzau in Nuuk. "I hope no one is in any doubt about that, either in the United States or the rest of the world."Trump's interest in Greenland has been a recurring theme on his social media accounts and in speeches since he took office again last year, claiming the island is necessary to the US to shore up its national security.His post came shortly after the European Commission announced a €200m (£172m) investment in the Danish territory during a visit by Commission president Ursula von der Leyen and Frederiksen. The European Commission said its investment would focus on education, internet connectivity, the use of raw materials in the country and hydropower energy.Meanwhile, Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum said Mexico "is neither nor will be a colony or protectorate of any foreign country," after Trump's post.  "Proudly we are a free, independent, and sovereign nation," she wrote on social media.

schema.headline: Iceland summons US ambassador over Trump's stars and stripes map

title: Monty Don to leave Gardeners' World after more than 20 years
description: Monty Don is to step down as the host of Gardeners' World after more than 20 years, the BBC has announced. The 71-year-old, who is the programme's lon
body: Monty Don is to step down as the host of Gardeners' World after more than 20 years, the BBC has announced. The 71-year-old, who is the programme's longest-serving head gardener, will leave at the end of the current series.In a statement, Don said working on the show had been a "deeply rewarding experience," but added: "Now is the right time for a change."The BBC said Don had "inspired and guided millions of viewers with his warmth, wisdom and passion for gardening" since joining the programme in 2003.Don began presenting the programme at Berryfields, a rented garden in Stratford-upon-Avon, before it moved in 2011 to his own garden, Longmeadow in Herefordshire. "Throughout that time - and around 700 programmes - I have had the privilege of sharing my own abiding passion for gardens and gardening with an equally passionate, and often equally knowledgeable audience," he said."That connection with millions, not just in Britain but across the world, who share a love of gardens, plants and the natural world is something I have always treasured and which I increasingly believe to be at the heart of a life well lived."Don added he had "always relished the craft of programme making" and paid tribute to the "superlative BBC team" he worked with over the years. "I look forward to continuing to work with and for the BBC on other projects, as well as following new avenues," he concluded. "And of course, I will still be gardening, dog by side, here at Longmeadow."The presenter, whose full name is George Montague Don, made his TV debut in 1989 with a gardening segment on ITV's This Morning.That led to further work on the BBC and Channel 4, a newspaper column, and the publication of more than 20 books about gardening authored by Don.He replaced Alan Titchmarsh on Gardeners' World in 2003, but took a break from the programme in 2008 as he recovered from a stroke.He has also presented other programmes including Around the World in 80 Gardens, My Dream Farm, Mastercrafts, Monty Don's Rhineland Gardens, and coverage of the Chelsea Flower Show.The BBC's chief content officer Kate Phillips described Don as "unique", adding he was "a wonderfully engaging broadcaster with a soothing, calm presence who has inspired so many"."Monty's decision to leave Gardeners' World is one I respect, but I'm still very sad he's leaving," she added."We are a nation full of budding gardeners, and his tips and advice have been invaluable to viewers for more than 20 years and have certainly helped me increase my knowledge as well as my plant survival rate!"I would like to thank Monty personally for his honesty and kindness which has seen him open up about his own personal struggles and the power of the natural world to improve mental health. We will miss him on the show hugely."Don has been open about his struggle with depression over the years.

schema.headline: Monty Don to leave Gardeners' World after more than 20 years

title: Glastonbury confirms ticket sale dates - and highest ever price
description: Image source, EPAImage caption, Olivia Rodrigo was the last act to perform on the Pyramid Stage in 2025, before Glastonbury took a fallow yearByMusic
body: Image source, EPAImage caption, Olivia Rodrigo was the last act to perform on the Pyramid Stage in 2025, before Glastonbury took a fallow yearByMusic correspondentUpdated 57 minutes agoAfter taking a fallow year in 2026, the Glastonbury Festival has confirmed that tickets for next year's event will go on sale in October.Tickets for the weekend will cost £408 including a £5 booking fee per ticket - an increase of £29.50 from 2025.Headliners for the festival, which takes place from 23 to 27 June, have yet to be announced, but rumours are already swirling, with everyone from Harry Styles and Fontaines DC to Taylor Swift and Stevie Wonder said to be in the mix.Tickets for the festival typically sell out in less than an hour, with thousands of fans  joining online queues to fight for their place.In a post on the official Glastonbury Instagram page, external, organisers said tickets with coach travel would go on sale at 18:00 BST on Thursday, 1 October.General admission tickets go on sale a couple of days later, at 09:00 BST on Sunday 4 October.As part of an ongoing campaign to stop touts, anyone wanting to attend Glastonbury had to be registered in advance. You can check your registration on its website. , externalIn recent years, the festival has also introduced an automatic queuing system on the day of sale, with fans needing to be online before the start of the sale with a valid registration number.Festival prices rise across the boardGlastonbury, which features more than 100 stages, was already the UK's most expensive music festival, but next year's ticket prices are the highest ever - breaking the £400 barrier for the first time.The increase is part of a pattern across the industry.Analysis by BBC News found the cost of attending the UK's major festivals has surged over the past decade - rising above the rate of inflation.Parklife tickets have increased by around £69 (71%) in real terms since 2013 - while Reading and Leeds had a much smaller increase, rising by about £40 (14%) over the same period.In the same period, Glastonbury's ticket prices went up by about £85  - a 30% price hike.The price hikes have multiple causes - from increased energy and infrastructure costs to post-Brexit labour shortages. However, last weekend's Reading and Leeds festival held prices at their 2025 level, with passes costing £325, rising to £361 with early-bird entry.Glastonbury said they would not be commenting on today's announcement but, in 2023, Emily Eavis acknowledged it was a "challenging time" for festival organisers."We have tried very hard to minimise the increase in price on the ticket but we're facing enormous rises in the costs of running this vast show, whilst still recovering from the huge financial impact of two years without a festival because of Covid."Image source, ReutersImage caption, Madonna has hinted that she will perform in the UK next year, but has not said whereThe festival last took place in 2025, with Olivia Rodrigo, The 1975 and Neil Young topping the bill.Glastonbury organiser Emily Eavis recently scotched rumours that Madonna would be among the headliners for next year's event."No, it's definitely not Madonna, I'll tell you that," she told BBC Radio 4's The Media Show."But we have got three [other] headliners and we're very excited about it - it's all coming together really well," she added.Asked about the possibility of a performance from Taylor Swift, Eavis laughed and said she didn't want to discuss the line-up any more.

schema.headline: Glastonbury confirms ticket sale dates - and highest ever price

title: A&E did not get the basics right - now my son's life is ruined at 32
description: In May 2024, a few months after having treatment for a brain tumour, Oli Coppock went to Warrington Hospital's emergency department with bad headaches
body: In May 2024, a few months after having treatment for a brain tumour, Oli Coppock went to Warrington Hospital's emergency department with bad headaches and dizziness.He underwent tests and assessments, but did not have a brain scan, before going home. It was a decision that ultimately ruined his life at the age of 32, his family says. A week later, with fluid building up on the brain, he suffered a cardiac arrest. He did not recover and now lives in almost complete paralysis.Oli's case is just one of a growing number of clinical negligence claims being made in England relating to A&E care. An analysis by the BBC shows there has been a 41% rise in cases over the past five years, with doctors linking it to the long delays and pressures being seen in emergency departments.Oli's father, Stephen, says he knows A&E staff are under pressure, but he cannot understand how a brain scan was not ordered, given his son's medical history.Despite the brain tumour and a recent diagnosis of multiple sclerosis, Oli was otherwise fit and well and positive about his future. He had a career in digital marketing, loved going to the gym and did some DJing in his spare time.Stephen says the whole family – including Oli's six siblings - has been left "angry and broken" by what happened to him. North Cheshire and Mersey NHS Foundation Trust, which runs Warrington's A&E, has now accepted a breach of duty in not ordering a CT brain scan, which on the balance of probabilities would have identified the fluid build-up in his brain and led to surgery to address it.In a statement, the trust said: "We are deeply sorry that Mr Coppock did not receive that standard of care that should be expected and we recognise the distress and lasting impact on patients and their families when harm is caused."An interim damages payment has been agreed. However, Oli's solicitor, Tanzeela Aslam, head of medical negligence at Express Solicitors, says the time taken to get to this point – more than two years – has just added to the failings, depriving him of access to funds for therapies and support that could have improved his quality of life."Oli's case illustrates how preventable errors within the NHS can have devastating and life-changing consequences for individuals and their families."She says she is seeing more and more A&E-related cases – something she too puts down to the growing pressures. "There has been an increased reliance on corridor care for patients, and we are seeing cases across A&E departments of misdiagnoses that have led to serious injury and in some cases death."A BBC analysis of NHS Resolution figures using published data and freedom of information requests showed there were more than 1,623 A&E-related clinical negligence claims in 2025-26 in England – up from 1,151 in 2020-21.It means A&E is now the single biggest area for clinical negligence claims in terms of number. The value of those claims exceeded £550m last year.Not all claims will result in damages being paid – that happens in about half of all cases. The NHS sometimes accepts liability but it is judged compensation is not needed.And there were points during the 2010s when the number of claims were higher per A&E attendance than they were now before falling.But the sustained increase over the past five years is causing concern, say experts. The pattern is not being repeated in other areas, such as maternity or orthopaedics, and the low point in 2020-21 is thought to be unrelated to any behaviour changes by patients during the Covid pandemic as it takes three years on average for a claim to be submitted.The Royal College of Emergency Medicine told the BBC it was worried about the rise, linking it to increasing pressure and long delays being seen in A&E in recent years. Over the last two years one in 10 patients who attended A&E spent more than 12 hours waiting to be treated or discharged.RCEM's Dr Adrian Boyle said the figures were "sobering". "This is a concern. But it is not surprising when you see how busy departments are. People are staying longer and pressure on staffing is increasing."But he said clinical negligence cases were still relatively rare – happening in only around one in every 17,000 attendances.NHS Resolution, which supports NHS trusts with clinical negligence claims, said it was taking action on the "high volume" of claims and has published reports to help the NHS learn from mistakes.Such mistakes include missing the signs of acute deterioration in patients, failing to order the necessary tests and scans and making incorrect diagnoses.NHS England said claim numbers were not a good measure of current safety because of the lag between the incident happening and claims being logged, adding there were signs A&E waiting times had started improving.Matthew Hopkins, of NHS Alliance, which represents hospitals, said health bosses were "making every effort is made to ensure safe, high-quality care, and that lessons are learned when that falls short".For Stephen, "every waking hour" is spent worrying about his son."I know staff are under pressure," he says, "but this is about doing the basics right. They failed Oli."Additional reporting Nat Wright

schema.headline: A&E did not get the basics right - now my son's life is ruined at 32

title: In West Bank, date farmers weigh impact of UK sanctions on Israeli settlers
description: Image caption, Dates are among the agricultural products commonly exported from Israeli settlements in the West BankByYolande KnellMiddle East corresp
body: Image caption, Dates are among the agricultural products commonly exported from Israeli settlements in the West BankByYolande KnellMiddle East correspondentUpdated 3 hours agoJuicy brown and ripening yellow dates dangle down from the branches of each palm tree at Israeli settler farms in the Jordan Valley, in the occupied West Bank.This year, as Israeli growers get ready for a good harvest, they are also preparing for the impact of new Western sanctions against settlements, which are illegal under international law.The UK government has announced an import ban on settlement goods and said it planned to take action against companies and individuals who provide services for settlement expansion, as part of what it calls a "comprehensive reset" of policy towards Israel following similar moves by several other European countries.Canada, Denmark, Finland, France, Iceland, Ireland, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Spain and Sweden have also confirmed their intention to introduce national restrictions, or support European restrictions, on trade in goods with settlements.Palestinians strongly back such a move, but Israel's foreign minister called it "hostile" and announced a series of counter measures, including the closure of the British consulate in East Jerusalem.Israeli date farmer Avigdor Arbel, from the settlement of Mesua, calls such boycotts "really disgusting".Arbel sells his produce mostly to Europe but also to the US and now, India. However, he says the sector is ready for any new UK ban on settler goods."As soon as we have a situation of pressure and boycotts, we always break out and look for other markets," he tells me. "So, I believe that if we get to a situation in which there's no place to sell my fruits in Europe, we'll find other markets."Image caption, Settler farmer Avigdor Arbel does not believe Israel will ever give up the Jordan ValleyWest Bank settlements have expanded rapidly under the current Israeli government, whose ministers say they want "to bury the idea" of an independent Palestinian state - part of the long-standing international formula for peace in the region known as the two-state solution.At the same time, settler violence against Palestinians has surged to what the UN says is "an all-time high".With new settler outposts - which are also illegal under Israeli law - now dotting the barren hilltops of the Jordan Valley, there have been repeated attacks on local Palestinians, particularly Bedouin and herding communities.In January, the last of some 600 villagers fled their homes in Ras Ein al-Ouja after intense harassment by hardline settlers, often backed by Israeli security forces. It was the largest single displacement of a Palestinian community in the past three years.Further north, in March, Israeli settlers brutally beat and sexually assaulted a Palestinian shepherd during a night raid on Khirbet Humsa.British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband told Parliament on Tuesday that a set of facts on the ground had been created "to make the two-state solution unviable," while "settler terrorism is rampant".Quoting a former Israeli minister of health and retired brigadier general, Ephraim Sneh, he said the UK government "agrees that there is ethnic cleansing of Palestinians in areas of the West Bank perpetrated by settler terrorists", to which the Israeli government had "turned a blind eye" or actually supported.In a significant change of UK policy, he said the government now agreed with the 2024 International Court of Justice advisory opinion that Israel's continued occupation "is unlawful".As a consequence, Miliband said this should be reflected "in the economic relationships we choose to have with the occupied territories"."I do not believe that the British people want us supporting the occupation by accepting products from settlements in our shops and supermarkets."Image caption, The Jordan Valley is a fertile strip of land that comprises nearly 30% of the West BankMedjool dates are the main export crop from both Israeli settler farms and Palestinian farms in the Jordan Valley."These are rubbish," says Palestinian farmer Abdul Halim Abu Omar, dramatically reaching up and throwing away a handful of shrivelled, yellow dates from a tree in the grove where he works in al-Ouja, north of Jericho.Around half of the date palms here have no fruit at all. "It's because we lack water," Abu Omar says. His is an extreme case: this year, the trees he cares for have received less than a third of the water they need to thrive.Access to water has long been a pressing issue in the West Bank. Interim peace agreements from the 1990s have left a water disparity between Israelis and Palestinians, and Israeli authorities typically prioritise water for settlers over Palestinians' needs. Recently, in rural areas of the Jordan Valley, almost all of which is under Israeli security and civilian control, extremist settlers have also taken over several freshwater springs.The Israeli Civil Administration told the BBC that it keeps "continuous contact" with the Palestinian Water Authority and assists in carrying out repairs to water infrastructure.This harvest time, Abu Omar has few dates that are fit to show local Palestinian exporter Momen Sinokrot. His firm, Palestine Gardens, works with 55 date growers in the Jordan Valley to sell to several European countries, including the UK.Sinokrot believes that if more states ban settlement trade this could curb settlement growth."Settlers are very active in the Jordan Valley... and they are not obeying any laws or rules or anything even from the Israeli army itself," he says. "They are going to the fields of the growers, they are stealing from them, and they are controlling more and more land."Image caption, Palestinian farmer Abdul Halim says half his date farms have no fruit because of a water shortageIsraeli-state support for settlements, as well as their relatively easy access to global markets, means that Palestinian farmers struggle to compete. Palestinian businesses face greater restrictions and costs to export across Israeli-controlled borders.Palestinians want the wide swathe of fertile land in the Jordan Valley - along the West Bank's border with Jordan - as part of their own hoped-for future state, along with the rest of the West Bank and Gaza, with East Jerusalem as its capital.However, Avigdor Arbel, the settler date farmer, does not believe that his country will ever give up the Jordan Valley. He has lived there since the 1970s.Within years of Israel's capture of the West Bank from Jordan in the 1967 Middle East War, the Israeli government began encouraging its citizens to move to this area to counter what it saw as the security risk along the border.More than 500,000 Israelis live in settlements in the West Bank, not including Israeli-annexed East Jerusalem, alongside three million Palestinians.There are 340 settler outposts in the Palestinian territory along with 146 settlements, formally recognised by the Israeli government, according to the Israeli anti-settlement group Peace Now.Current UK and EU laws require labels for settlement goods. Agricultural produce commonly exported includes mangoes, avocados, herbs and grapes.Image caption, Israeli settlers diverted a Palestinian village's water to fill a pool in the Jordan Valley this summerThere have been questions raised about how a ban on settlement goods would be enforced.A recent report by the legal advocacy group Global Echo found that some settlement fruits and vegetables sold in Europe were inaccurately identified as coming from Israel - or mingled with produce from inside Israel's internationally-recognised borders.However, the report's author, Jessica Stober, suggests that a UK ban on settler goods would greatly increase the financial costs associated with any such fraudulent practices. Instead of a seller being fined for misrepresenting their goods, the shipment would be returned."A ban is more self-enforcing because you have involved the private sector and it becomes commercially unviable for them to deal in settlement goods," Stober says."I would also say that a whole new set of measures become available to the UK government under a sanctions regime, under a ban, including civil and criminal penalties that make compliance much more likely."Image caption, Palestinian exporter Momen Sinokrot believes sanctions could help curb settlement growthIsrael's Foreign Minister, Gideon Saar, responded quickly to the UK's announcement, branding the move "morally distorted" and constituting a "blatant interference in the affairs of a sovereign state and in its electoral process", referring to Israel's general election in late October.He announced "a series of Israeli countermeasures", including the closure of the British consulate in Jerusalem and the removal of British representatives from the US-led International Gaza Support Center (IGSC) in Kiryat Gat, which is in charge of co-ordinating the shaky ceasefire in the Gaza Strip."The message to every government that harms us is clear: whoever acts against Israel, Israel will act against them, and they will lose their influence and relevance in the region," Saar warned.Last month, Israel expelled two Dutch diplomats from the IGSC, after the Netherlands banned trade from settlements.Other European countries that have already imposed a ban on settlement goods or trade restrictions - arguing it is a legal obligation - include Ireland, Spain and Belgium.Now, the new action by the UK looks set to put a new, heavy strain on its relations with Israel.

schema.headline: In West Bank, date farmers weigh impact of UK sanctions on Israeli settlers

title: Two ports denied request to land 120 migrants in RNLI boats
description: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The King's Harbour Master Portsmouth declined a request to allow the migrants into the harbour, the BBC under
body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The King's Harbour Master Portsmouth declined a request to allow the migrants into the harbour, the BBC understandsByNikki MitchellSouth of England home affairs correspondent and Stuart RustSouth of EnglandUpdated 3 hours agoRequests to accept the landing of RNLI boats carrying 120 migrants intercepted off the Isle of Wight were refused by both Portsmouth harbour and Southampton Port.When the migrants were landed on Sunday at Eastney, in Langstone Harbour, anti-migrant protesters blocked the road.Associated British Ports (ABP), which operates Southampton, said it was not the closest port and it "did not have suitable reception facilities available".The BBC understands the King's Harbour Master (KHM) Portsmouth also declined a coastguard request, but it would not comment directly on operational matters. The protest followed a separate demonstration at the Port of Dover on the previous day.The Langstone Harbour Master said the migrants were "recovered" onto two RNLI vessels in the vicinity of the Nab Tower.They said they would have travelled at "quite a slow speed" to Langstone because the vessels were so overloaded.An RNLI spokesperson said: "We are working with the relevant parties to understand the decision to deny access, and we are disappointed with the nature of the communication with our crews, who voluntarily give their time to save the lives of others at sea."Image caption, Hundreds of people protested in Portsmouth after migrants were brought ashore on SundayThe narrow peninsula at Eastney has only one road leading in and out, which demonstrators used to block coaches carrying the migrants from leaving the area.It led to a stand-off that lasted into the early hours of Monday.Portsmouth City Council said it was a "completely unsuitable location to bring the boats ashore" and brought "needless disruption" to the area.Langstone Harbour Master Billy Johnson said the coastguard was coordinating "a search and rescue operation" and there was "no reason not to accept" the landing of the vessels at Eastney."The problem was managing the public order aspect that was also taking place and the geography of the area made that very challenging for the police," he said."This is a new thing in the Solent and the degree to which it attracted public interest  and the speed at which the public reaction was mobilised was unusual and surprising."The way the emergency services mobilised was really effective, with the police, Border Force, coastguard, the RNLI, ambulance and fire service working completely together - all of whom were hindered by the activities of protesters."ABP said it received an enquiry about landing recovered migrants.It said in a statement: "We had to decline the enquiry as the Port did not have suitable reception facilities available. "If there had been a safety of life at sea issue where Southampton was the closest port or if we had received a formal direction from the relevant authority then we would have played a role."Neither was the case in this situation."'Fear and tension'The leader of Portsmouth City Council, Steve Pitt, said: "The Home Office has some serious questions to answer about their lack of planning, inconsistent decision-making and ultimately, poor judgement."In the House of Commons yesterday, Dame Caroline Dinenage, Conservative MP for Gosport, referred to the boat containing 120 migrants in the Solent as an "extraordinary mega dinghy".She said: "MPs across the Solent region were scrambling for reliable information with complete radio silence from the Home Office. As a result we weren't in a position to calm fear and tension."Responding for the government, Home Office minister Sarah Jones said the department would "learn any lessons that we need to" following the weekend's protests. Asked why Eastney had been chosen as the landing site, she said: "We are of course making sure we understand what exactly happened in that circumstance."Get in touchYour Voice

schema.headline: Two ports denied request to land 120 migrants in RNLI boats

title: Ballon d'Or 2026 nominees: Harry Kane, Jude Bellingham and Declan Rice nominated
description: Bayern Munich striker Harry Kane is one of three England players nominated for the 2026 Ballon d'Or.Real Madrid's Jude Bellingham and Arsenal's Declan
body: Bayern Munich striker Harry Kane is one of three England players nominated for the 2026 Ballon d'Or.Real Madrid's Jude Bellingham and Arsenal's Declan Rice join Kane, the favourite for the award, on the 30-player shortlist.Inter Miami forward Lionel Messi, who is looking to win his ninth Ballon d'Or, has been nominated.The 39-year-old scored eight goals as Argentina lost the World Cup final to Spain in July, with Messi since retiring from international football.Lamine Yamal is one of six Spain players that won the World Cup to be included.Having scored the winning goal in the final, Paris St-Germain forward Ferran Torres, who joined the French club from Barcelona in the summer, makes the cut.Back-to-back Champions League winners Paris St-Germain have nine players - excluding new signing Torres - nominated, including last year's winner Ousmane Dembele.Real Madrid forwards Kylian Mbappe and Vinicius Jr also make the shortlist, as do Arsenal defenders Gabriel and William Saliba.The award is celebrating its 70th anniversary, having been created by France Football in 1956, and the winner will be announced at an ceremony in London on 26 October.The "symbolic choice of venue" is in tribute to former England player Sir Stanley Matthews, who won the first Ballon d'Or.

schema.headline: Ballon d'Or 2026 nominees: Harry Kane, Jude Bellingham and Declan Rice nominated

title: Liam Gallagher's tambourine grin and Charli XCX says bye to Brat - Music Photography Awards 2026 shortlist
description: Striking images of Oasis's reunion tour and Charli XCX bringing Brat to Glastonbury Festival are among the nominees at this year's Abbey Road Music Ph
body: Striking images of Oasis's reunion tour and Charli XCX bringing Brat to Glastonbury Festival are among the nominees at this year's Abbey Road Music Photography Awards.The awards, which this year considered works by more than 24,500 submissions from 42 different countries, released a shortlist of 40 finalists across eight categories on Tuesday.The likes of Kendrick Lamar, Fontaines DC, Tame Impala and Sombr also feature in the shots, while other images of stars including FKA Twigs have been selected - out of competition - for judges' awards.All of the finalist photographs will go on display in the LED tunnel at entertainment complex Outernet London from 8 to 14 September.These will include the five pieces picked out for consideration in the fan-voted music moment of the year award.Voting is available online via the official website, external, and in person at the exhibition.The winners will be announced at a ceremony at the London studios - made famous by the 1969 Beatles album of the same name - on 24 September.

schema.headline: Liam Gallagher's tambourine grin and Charli XCX says bye to Brat - Music Photography Awards 2026 shortlist

title: Nottingham attacks victim's death potentially preventable, inquiry hears
description: The death of a student killed in the Nottingham attacks was "potentially preventable", a public inquiry has heard.Barnaby Webber - along with Grace O'
body: The death of a student killed in the Nottingham attacks was "potentially preventable", a public inquiry has heard.Barnaby Webber - along with Grace O'Malley-Kumar and Ian Coates - were killed by Valdo Calocane, who had been diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia in 2020, on 13 June 2023.On Tuesday, ahead of closing statements to the Nottingham Inquiry, external - which is examining the killings - the inquiry was told a "more rapid administration of blood products" could have meant Barnaby's death was "potentially preventable".The inquiry also heard documents found in a bin at Calocane's address contained a list of explosives, which was not disclosed by Nottinghamshire Police until June this year.A panel of medical professionals assessed the emergency medical response on the day of the attacks to assess "survivability", the inquiry was told.In their assessment, the panel noted the hard work of the emergency responders in their care to the victims.The panel found if blood products had been administered to Barnaby earlier and more rapidly, it could have increased his chances of getting to hospital with enough of a heartbeat to undergo surgery.However, multiple other rapid and particular steps would have had to have taken place for him to have survived. The inquiry heard Barnaby had a less than 50% chance of surviving his injuries, characterised as "potentially preventable", while Grace and Ian's deaths were "not preventable".The families of the victims sobbed as the assessments were read out by counsel to the inquiry Rachel Langdale KC. Grace's father, Dr Sanjoy Kumar, left the hearing room. Langdale said Nottinghamshire Police found the documents in a bin at Calocane's former property in Burford Road in Nottingham.He wrote bullet points on one page about explosives under the heading "thoughts", including TNT and nitrate fertiliser.Langdale said: "This piece of paper listing thoughts about a number of explosives was not identified or taken into account at the time."She added it had not been made available by police to the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) or to psychiatric experts.Calocane was evicted from the Burford Road address on 11 June 2023 and travelled to London, before returning via to Nottingham shortly before midnight on 12 June, a day before his killings, the inquiry heard.The Nottingham Inquiry started hearing evidence in February, with more than 100 witnesses questioned over three months.Witnesses included police staff and officers, mental healthcare practitioners, Calocane's former flatmates and family members, the bereaved families and the survivors of the attacks. A number of revelations emerged in evidence about errors in Calocane's care, his previous interactions with police and failings both during and in the aftermath of the attacks. Calocane - who also seriously injured three others - is currently serving an indefinite hospital order in a high-security facility after pleading guilty to three counts of manslaughter, on the grounds of diminished responsibility, and to three counts of attempted murder.The inquiry is currently hearing updates in evidence since the end of oral evidence earlier this year. In her closing remarks, Langdale reiterated the evidence of former parliamentary ombudsman Sir Rob Behrens.She said: "Too often these cases are dependent upon bereaved families campaigning at a time when they are least prepared to do so, and it is an outstanding public service that they perform."Langdale added: "Although Sir Rob was talking generally about bereaved families, his words could have been written as a description of the bereaved families and their legal team in this inquiry. Indeed, without their efforts there would not have been a public inquiry at all."The evidence we have obtained has revealed one failure after another."There is a suggestion in some submissions that further oral evidence should be called. We submit that there's no need for further oral evidence from any source."Barney, Grace and Ian should be alive. And the survivors - uninjured."Final submissions to the chair, senior judge Deborah Taylor KC, will continue on Wednesday.Taylor said it was "disappointing" that over the break, evidence had emerged which "ought to have been identified" and disclosed earlier. She directed core participants to provide any corrections to errors or omissions by no later than 31 December.Langdale said Nottinghamshire Police also recovered a holdall bag belonging to Calocane - who is being referred to in the inquiry as VC - from his address in the days after the attacks.There were three notebooks in the bag, which included a note written by Calocane saying he was a god and "was a tree that guards the key between heaven and hell".In his closing speech, Tim Moloney KC, who represents the bereaved families, said a note made by Calocane on one of the sheets of paper appeared to say "Manchester Arena".Calocane searched online for large venues in Nottingham and bookmarks on his web browser for the Albert Hall Conference Centre in the city and the Theatre Royal and Royal Concert Hall, the inquiry heard.Moloney said the notebooks also revealed "relevant information including what we say was a deep-seated misogyny".The items were not prioritised because efforts were focused on finding a bag which the killer had with him on the evening of the attacks, the inquiry heard."There was a failure to investigate VC's historical behaviour and actions," Moloney said.He added "no-one asked VC why he was searching for explosives and large venues because they couldn't", referencing the police's failure to share the information.Langdale described the failure to disclose the notebooks an "oversight by Nottinghamshire Police".The inquiry heard further violent assaults by Calocane on colleagues at warehouses in Nottinghamshire were also not disclosed to the inquiry team until after the public hearings took place.This included an assault on a colleague in a warehouse in Eastwood in 2021 and another in Normanton in February 2023. Footage of the February 2023 attack, described by Moloney as "sustained attack with punches thrown", was shown to the inquiry for the first time on Tuesday. In his closing statement, Moloney focused on the timeline of contact between Calocane and public services."We say the timeline contains a litany of unnoticed red flags, missed opportunities and individual and systemic failures," he said."The bereaved families firmly believe that if opportunities had been taken to effectively deal with the behaviour of VC, if there had not been so many failures by so many people in institutions between 24 May 2020 and 13 June 2023, then their loved ones would still be here today."They have good reason to believe that, because VC's history of contact with public agencies is one of repeated individual and systemic failures in the face of the clear and growing risk that he presented."Moloney said there were failures by authorities to follow policies and procedures and adequately consider harm with "every incident" involving Calocane between 2022 and 2023."Police were too quick to let things go in the teeth of really quite serious incidents, and clinicians were too quick to adopt a least restrictive practice which ignored the rights of his victims as we say ultimately and the rights of the public," he said. "Together, these practices diverted VC away from the criminal justice system or forensic psychiatry and he should have been going down that pathway. "Together, these practices failed VC and the people he affected who sit in this room."

schema.headline: Nottingham attacks victim's death potentially preventable, inquiry hears

title: Lindsay Clancy's lawyer hopes for deal with prosecutors after mistrial
description: The lawyer for the Massachusetts woman accused of murdering her three children says he hopes to reach an agreement with prosecutors, after the case en
body: The lawyer for the Massachusetts woman accused of murdering her three children says he hopes to reach an agreement with prosecutors, after the case ended in a mistrial on Friday. Kevin Reddington told ABC's Good Morning America programme that he was upset a lone member of the jury would not acquit Lindsay Clancy. To find Clancy guilty, jurors had to be unanimously convinced beyond a reasonable doubt that she intentionally killed her children - Cora, Dawson and Callan - and was not experiencing a psychotic break.On ABC, Reddington also appealed to President Donald Trump to pardon Clancy. Because she was charged by the state, though, only the Massachusetts governor has the power to pardon her."I would hope that you [Trump] would consider this young lady, the type of person she is, what she's been through, and consider a pardon," Reddington said.Reddington also said he hoped the district attorney prosecuting the case "would be able to work something out that would be acceptable to both sides".The BBC has contacted the district attorney for Plymouth County, Massachusetts."I'm willing to listen to Tim," Reddington said about District Attorney Tim Cruz, calling him a "hard-charging prosecutor".The jury - nine women and three men - was weighing a range of options, from not guilty by reason of insanity to manslaughter and first-degree murder. The 12-member panel appeared to nearly reach a consensus, except for a single holdout who, Reddington said, "would not apply the law of reasonable doubt" as instructed by the judge."That's not right," he said. "And that's why I was upset." Throughout the trial, prosecutors called dozens of witnesses, including several doctors, seeking to prove Clancy had made a calculated decision to murder her children in the basement of their Massachusetts home in January 2023.Clancy does not deny killing the three, but says there was no premeditation and she was experiencing psychosis at the time. For her to be convicted of first-degree murder, a jury would have to believe she planned the killings.The BBC has contacted the governor's office about a possible pardon request.Under Massachusetts law, Reddington could also formally ask the judge to rule independently that Clancy was not guilty based on evidence presented during the trial. He has five days to file that motion. Currently, the case rests with the prosecution, who must decide whether to seek another trial.With additional reporting from Ione Wells

title: Harry and Meghan 'surprised' by King's letter making clear they remain non-working royals
description: A spokesperson for the Duke and Duchess of Sussex says the couple were surprised to see a letter sent on behalf of King Charles clarifying that Prince
body: A spokesperson for the Duke and Duchess of Sussex says the couple were surprised to see a letter sent on behalf of King Charles clarifying that Prince Harry and Meghan remained non-working royals.The spokesperson said the couple, who have recently moved back to the UK, "were a little surprised not to have been told about this in advance".But royal sources say Prince Harry and Meghan were made aware of the letter, sent on Monday afternoon, before it was made public.It is also understood a security committee, which includes Home Office representatives, is meeting this week to look at the level of taxpayer-funded security that should be given to the Sussexes who are now resident in the UK.The Royal and VIP Executive Committee - known as Ravec - decides security for royals and public figures and Prince Harry has previously complained about a lack of adequate police protection in the UK.The Home Office does not comment on such decision making - and would be unlikely to reveal the outcome of such a meeting."The UK government's protective security system is rigorous and proportionate. It is our long-standing policy not to provide detailed information on those arrangements, as doing so could compromise their integrity and affect individuals' security," said a Home Office spokesperson.In terms of Prince Harry and Meghan being "surprised" by the King's message on Monday - it's understood that reflects the lack of time given to them to respond.They were believed to have had only had sight of the letter about an hour before it was shared with the media. By the time his team had made contact with Prince Harry it's understood the letter was almost published.The letter, sent on behalf of the King, spelt out the non-working royal status of Prince Harry and Meghan, who moved back from California with children Archie and Lilibet last month.They will still not be able to use titles of "His and Her Royal Highness", and remain "private citizens", says the letter sent on behalf of the King by the Lord Chamberlain, a top Palace official.The letter was sent to Prince Harry's team, government departments, military officials and Lord Lieutenants, according to Palace sources.Lord Lieutenants, who are the monarch's local representatives, and government staff are often involved in royal visits and engagements.This letter makes clear that any engagements carried out by the Sussexes will be in a private capacity and they will not be representing the Royal Family.It seems to be something of a shot across the bows, making clear that any Prince Harry and Meghan visits should not be treated as royal engagements.This comes ahead of what are likely to be public appearances by the Sussexes this autumn, as they settle in the UK and support their charities.

schema.headline: Harry and Meghan 'surprised' by King's letter making clear they remain non-working royals

title: Renoir paintings worth millions stolen in French museum heist
description: Two paintings by the impressionist artist Pierre-Auguste Renoir have been stolen from a museum in the south of France.Two thieves broke into the Renoi
body: Two paintings by the impressionist artist Pierre-Auguste Renoir have been stolen from a museum in the south of France.Two thieves broke into the Renoir Museum in Cagnes-sur-Mer early on Tuesday, seizing four paintings but dropping two of the works in the museum gardens as they escaped, local Mayor Bryan Masson said.The paintings, each worth €9m (£7.7m; $10.4m), are the latest high-profile pieces to have been stolen in a string of recent heists in Europe which have thrust the security of art in galleries and museums into the spotlight.One of the most high-profile was in October last year, when a brazen heist at the Louvre Museum in Paris saw France's priceless crown jewels being stolen.CCTV footage captured the thieves entering the Renoir museum gardens by cutting through a fence before they cut through structures holding the paintings' frames in place, the local mayor said.The alarm went off at 05:48 (05:48 GMT), and police were at the scene within five minutes, Masson explained, saying the thieves fled the scene upon hearing the security alarms.He later told reporters that the thieves seemed to be "well-equipped" and "well-informed".They were "wearing helmets, gloves, and combat gear" and carrying "an electric knife and hacksaw," he added.Investigators have found two zip-up bags at the scene, which may have belonged to the suspects.

schema.headline: Renoir paintings worth millions stolen in French museum heist
